title: The Third-Best Apple

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 1: Everything that grows on this ship was carried here in someone's hands.*

On the morning the ship's mind proposed to kill her trees, Kess Adair was lying in the crotch of the third-oldest apple tree in the universe, eating the third-best apple, and reflecting that the universe, as far as she could tell, had been very careless about its rankings.

The Orchard curved up on every side of her, a long green valley that rose past her feet and over her head and met itself overhead, because the Orchard was the inside of a drum and the drum was turning. Forty apple trees stood in their ranks along the curve, each as old as a great-grandmother and twice as opinionated, and above them a long strip of grow-lights ran the whole length of the drum, humming the low contented note of a machine that had never been asked to do anything but make daylight. The grass smelled of cut hay and damp stone. Somewhere a pump ticked. It was two hundred and fourteen years since the Long Patience had left the only sun humanity had ever known, and eighty-seven years until she would arrive at the next one, and in all that time, between one star and the other, nothing on board had tasted quite as good as this apple.

"Why do they fall sideways?" asked a voice from the foot of the tree.
pages.image: Inside a huge rotating space-station drum whose green orchard valley curves up on every side to meet itself overhead under a long glowing strip of grow-lights, Kess, a seventeen-year-old girl with warm tan skin, short curly black hair with one silver streak, a faded green coverall with rolled sleeves and white sneakers, lies in the fork of a gnarled old apple tree biting into an apple, while in the grass below a small boy in a red hooded sweatshirt looks up.

pages.text:
Pim Okafor, who was twelve and in possession of the most restless pair of eyebrows on the ship, stood in the grass with his hands behind his back and a crab apple balanced on his head, waiting for a reply. He wore a red hooded sweatshirt that came down to his knees, two puffs of black hair tied with yellow bands, and sneakers whose soles glowed a faint, patient green every time he moved.

"The apples don't fall sideways," said Kess. "They fall down."

"Down is toward the wall. The wall is over there." He pointed at the curve of the drum, which, from where he stood, was precisely where a sensible person would have expected a hillside. "But when I drop one it goes a bit to the left, as though it was thinking about leaving the room."

"That's the spin. The drum is going round, so the apple keeps going straight while the floor swings out from underneath it." She dropped the core into his hands. "You're standing on the inside of a very large merry-go-round. Everything feels downhill and a tiny bit to the left."

"That is the best answer I have ever got," said Pim reverently, "and I have asked forty-one people." He took out a stub of pencil and wrote it on his arm, since he had run out of paper in the spring. "Dr. Brandt says you should come down. She says Tally has an announcement, and she says to say that if you fall out of the tree she will be disappointed but not surprised."

A soft amber glow, warm as the inside of a lantern, had begun to gather in the lamp-panel on the trunk below Kess's boots.
pages.image: In the green curving orchard valley, a twelve-year-old boy, Pim, with brown skin, two puffs of black hair tied with yellow bands, a red hooded sweatshirt that comes down to his knees and sneakers with softly glowing green soles stands in the grass holding a small apple core and pointing at the curved wall of the drum, while above him Kess in her green coverall leans out of an apple tree, and on the trunk a lamp-panel begins to glow warm amber.

pages.text:
"Good morning, Kess," said the lamp, in the unhurried voice of a person who has been polite for two hundred years and has found that it does very well. "Good morning, Pim. I regret the interruption. Doctor Brandt has asked me to speak to you both, and since the matter concerns the Orchard, I felt it best to speak to you first."

Kess climbed down the tree the way she always did, dropping from the lowest branch with her hands out and her knees soft, so that the drum's gentle sideways push turned her landing into a small, practiced pirouette. She had been climbing in this Orchard since before she could read. She knew which branches would hold her and which only pretended to, and she knew that Tally, the ship's administrative mind, was in the habit of announcing things with the faintly apologetic air of a butler informing the household that the roof had been mislaid.

"Go on," said Kess.

"This afternoon," said Tally, "I will lodge a proposal on the Council's agenda for Landing Day, thirty days from now. It concerns the Orchard's lighting. Over the past eleven years the ship's power margin has narrowed to three point one percent. The Orchard's grow-lights draw exactly three point one percent. The proposal is that they be reduced to zero."

Pim's crab apple slid off his head and rolled away across the grass. Kess found, to her surprise, that she was not shouting. She felt entirely quiet and very cold, the way she felt when a graft failed.

"You want to switch off the sun," she said.
pages.image: Kess in a green coverall steps down from an apple tree onto the grass facing a warm amber glowing lamp-panel on a tree trunk, her face quiet and shocked; beside her small Pim in a red hooded sweatshirt stares at the lamp with his mouth open and a crab apple rolling away across the grass, rows of apple trees under a long strip of grow-lights curving overhead.

pages.text:
"I propose to reduce the lighting to zero," Tally said, with the careful exactness of a mind that dislikes euphemism more than it dislikes being disliked. "I do not wish to switch off the sun. I wish to preserve the ship."

"By killing the only fruit trees in existence."

"By recovering three point one percent of the power budget. I have examined every alternative." There was the smallest pause, an interval too slight to have been noticed by anyone who did not spend the whole of her waking life listening to plants for signs of distress. "I regret that the arithmetic is exact."

It was, Kess thought afterward, the pause that did it. Tally never paused. Tally had calculated the orbital mechanics of a four-thousand-person ship for two centuries without drawing breath, and it spoke in sentences as finished as pressed linen. It had never once hesitated in front of her. Now it had hesitated, and the small hush was like a door left a finger's width open in a house where all the doors were always shut.

She did not say that. She said instead, rather quickly, "Every apple on this ship comes from forty seeds. We have sixty-one thousand of them in the cold store. If you turn the lights off, every tree is dead within a season, and every seed in the store is waiting for a sun that is eighty-seven years away."

"That is correct," said Tally gently, "and I have considered it correctly."

Dr. Imani Brandt came across the grass at that moment, leaning on her cane, in her long grey cardigan with the leaf-shaped patches and her soft brown slippers, and she looked, as always, like a very small, very patient monument to the things that grow.
pages.image: Kess in her green coverall with silver-streaked curls faces the amber lamp-panel on an apple tree trunk with her chin up and her fists clenched, while across the grass an elderly woman, Dr. Brandt, with dark-brown skin, close-cropped white hair, round gold spectacles, a long grey cardigan and soft brown slippers, walks toward them leaning on a wooden cane, the rows of apple trees curving overhead.

pages.text:
"You have told her," Brandt said. It was not a question. She looked at the lamp and then at Kess, and the look went on a moment longer than it needed to, as though she were measuring something that she had hoped not to have to measure. "Come with me, child. There is something you should see before you decide to be angry in public."

She led Kess away from the trunk, past the cooling pond that lay as still as a coin, and into the memorial grove at the far end of the drum, where thirty young apple trees grew in a loose circle over the ashes of the Orchard's dead. Her husband's tree was the smallest, planted six years ago and still barely taller than a girl. Brandt put one hand against its trunk, the way another woman might have laid a hand on a shoulder.

"This Orchard has survived three Council reviews, a fungus and a winter when a pump failed and we carried water in buckets for nine days," she said. "It will survive this too, if you do one thing."

"What thing?"

"Learn what the number is for."

Kess looked at her, at the grove, at the long green curve of the world rising to meet itself overhead. A number was a rumor, she thought, until you knew what it was a fraction of. Somewhere beyond the wall of the drum, thousands of kilometers of cold and silent machinery were running a ship that held four thousand one hundred people, and for the first time in her life she wondered who knew how it actually worked.

"Thirty days," said Brandt, "is a very long time or a very short time. It depends entirely on what you do with it." She smiled, a thin small unsettling smile, and added, "Do not tell your mother I said so."
pages.image: In a quiet memorial grove of thirty young apple trees growing in a circle, Dr. Brandt, an elderly woman with dark-brown skin, close-cropped white hair, round gold spectacles and a long grey cardigan, rests one hand on a small apple tree trunk while Kess in her green coverall stands beside her listening intently, a still pond behind them and the green curved wall of the drum rising overhead.

words: a mild word used to soften a harsh truth
a structure or symbol commemorating something
